questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the tangent ratio of an acute angle is defined as:
options: opposite ÷ adjacent
opposite ÷ hypotenuse
adjacent ÷ hypotenuse
hypotenuse ÷ opposite
questions.explanation: Tangent compares the side opposite the angle with the side adjacent to it (not the hypotenuse), so tan = opposite/adjacent. The option opposite ÷ hypotenuse is the sine ratio, which is the most common mix-up. Remember that tangent is the only one of the three basic ratios that never involves the hypotenuse.

questions.stem: Two right-angled triangles each contain an angle of 35°. What must be true about them?
options: They are similar only if one side length is shared
Their side ratios differ because their sizes differ
They are similar, so their matching side ratios are equal
They are congruent, so their matching sides are equal in length
questions.explanation: Both triangles have a 90° angle and a 35° angle, so the third angles must also match, making the triangles equiangular and therefore similar. Similar triangles have all corresponding sides in the same ratio, so ratios such as opposite/hypotenuse are identical. Saying they are congruent is wrong because equal angles fix the shape but not the size — congruence also needs a matching side length.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle is enlarged by a scale factor of 4. What happens to the sine of one of its acute angles?
options: It becomes 16 times larger
It becomes 4 times smaller
It stays exactly the same
It becomes 4 times larger
questions.explanation: Enlargement multiplies both the opposite side and the hypotenuse by 4, so the ratio opposite/hypotenuse is unchanged — the 4s cancel. Choosing 4 times larger applies the scale factor to a ratio rather than to individual lengths. The cue is that trigonometric ratios depend only on the angle, never on the size of the triangle.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the cosine of an acute angle is:
options: the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse
the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse
the adjacent side divided by the opposite side
the hypotenuse divided by the adjacent side
questions.explanation: Cosine compares the side next to the angle with the longest side, so cos = adjacent/hypotenuse. The option opposite side divided by the hypotenuse is the sine ratio. Keep the order in mind: for both sine and cosine the hypotenuse is the denominator.

questions.stem: Triangle ABC has a right angle at B, with AB = 3 cm, BC = 4 cm and AC = 5 cm. Triangle PQR is similar to ABC with PQ = 6 cm, QR = 8 cm and PR = 10 cm. The sine of angle C in triangle ABC is 0.6. What is the sine of angle R in triangle PQR?
questions.explanation: Angle R corresponds to angle C, and similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and equal side ratios, so sin R = 6/10 = 0.6, the same value. Choosing 1.2 comes from doubling the ratio along with the side lengths, but doubling both the numerator and denominator leaves the ratio unchanged. The value 0.75 comes from dividing the two shorter sides instead of using the hypotenuse.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has an acute angle θ with adjacent side 5 cm and hypotenuse 13 cm. A second right-angled triangle also contains angle θ and has hypotenuse 39 cm. What is the length of the side adjacent to θ in the second triangle?
options: 15 cm
5 cm
36 cm
13 cm
questions.explanation: Since cos θ = 5/13 is constant for the angle θ, the adjacent side is 5/13 of the hypotenuse: 5/13 × 39 = 15 cm. Answering 5 cm assumes the side length itself is fixed, when it is the ratio that is fixed. The hypotenuse has been tripled, so every side of the similar triangle is tripled.

questions.stem: Why does every right-angled triangle containing a 62° angle give the same value for tan 62°?
options: All such triangles are congruent, so corresponding sides are equal
Tangent is defined only for triangles with a hypotenuse of 1
The angles of every triangle add to 180°, so all ratios match
All such triangles are similar, so corresponding side ratios are equal
questions.explanation: A 90° angle plus a 62° angle forces the third angle to be 28°, so all such triangles are equiangular and therefore similar, giving identical ratios of corresponding sides. The congruence option is wrong because these triangles can be any size — equal angles do not fix side lengths. The angle sum fact explains why they are similar, but on its own it does not make ratios equal, since all triangles have an angle sum of 180°.

questions.stem: Triangle 1 has legs 5 cm and 12 cm. Triangle 2 has legs 20 cm and 48 cm. Both are right-angled. Which statement is correct?
options: The triangles are not similar, because no side lengths are shared
The triangles are similar, so their acute angles are equal in pairs
The triangles are congruent, since the legs are in the same ratio
The angles in Triangle 2 are 4 times the angles in Triangle 1
questions.explanation: Both pairs of legs are in the ratio 1:4 and the included angle is 90° in each, so the triangles are similar by two sides in proportion with the included angle equal, giving equal matching angles. Saying the angles are 4 times larger confuses enlarging lengths with enlarging angles — enlargement never changes angle size. Similarity requires proportional sides, not shared side lengths.

questions.stem: A student measures the angle of elevation to the top of a flagpole as 38° and draws a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 10 cm. A classmate draws the same 38° triangle with hypotenuse 25 cm. Comparing the two drawings:
options: The value of sin 38° found from each drawing is the same
The larger drawing gives a larger value of sin 38°
The larger drawing gives a smaller value of sin 38°
Only the 10 cm drawing can be used, since sine needs a small hypotenuse
questions.explanation: The two drawings are similar triangles, so opposite/hypotenuse gives the same value in each: the opposite side in the larger drawing is 2.5 times longer, but so is the hypotenuse. Thinking the larger drawing gives a larger sine confuses the length of a side with the value of a ratio. Sine is a ratio, so it is a pure number with no units and no dependence on scale.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, angle θ has sin θ = 0.6 and the hypotenuse is 20 cm. How long is the side opposite θ?
options: 16 cm
12 cm
questions.explanation: Since sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, the opposite side is 0.6 × 20 = 12 cm. The answer 16 cm is the adjacent side, found using cos θ = 0.8, so it answers a different question. Read carefully which side the ratio names before multiplying.

questions.stem: Two similar right-angled triangles have hypotenuses of 8 cm and 20 cm. In the smaller triangle the side opposite angle θ is 4.8 cm. What is tan θ?
questions.explanation: In the smaller triangle sin θ = 4.8/8 = 0.6, so by Pythagoras the adjacent side is √(8² − 4.8²) = 6.4 cm, giving tan θ = 4.8/6.4 = 0.75. The value 0.6 is sin θ, which is tempting because it is the first ratio calculated, but tangent needs the adjacent side, not the hypotenuse. The larger triangle gives the same answer, since similarity keeps all ratios constant.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has an acute angle θ with tan θ = 3/4. A similar triangle has its side adjacent to θ measuring 24 cm. What is the length of the hypotenuse of the larger triangle?
options: 18 cm
32 cm
40 cm
30 cm
questions.explanation: Since tan θ = opposite/adjacent = 3/4, the smaller triangle is a 3-4-5 triangle, and an adjacent side of 24 cm means a scale factor of 6, so the hypotenuse is 5 × 6 = 30 cm. Answering 18 cm gives the opposite side (3 × 6) rather than the hypotenuse. Identify the scale factor first, then multiply the side you actually need.

questions.stem: Two right-angled triangles each have a 41° angle. Why must their sine, cosine and tangent match?
options: Having two equal angles means each corresponding side differs by a fixed amount added on
Any two right-angled triangles are similar, whatever their acute angles
They share two equal angles, so they are similar and sides are in the same ratio
They are congruent, so their side lengths are identical
questions.explanation: Because the angles of a triangle sum to 180°, matching the right angle and the 41° angle forces the third angles to match too, so the triangles are similar by AA. Similarity means corresponding sides are in a constant ratio, so opposite/hypotenuse, adjacent/hypotenuse and opposite/adjacent take the same values in both — that is why sin 41°, cos 41° and tan 41° are fixed numbers. The claim that they are congruent with identical side lengths is tempting but wrong: equal angles fix the shape, not the size, and no side lengths were given. The cue is that similarity multiplies every side by the same scale factor, which cancels in a ratio, while congruence would require equal lengths.

questions.stem: Two right-angled triangles both contain the acute angle θ. In the smaller triangle the side opposite θ is 9 cm and the hypotenuse is 15 cm. In the larger triangle the side opposite θ is 21 cm. How long is the hypotenuse of the larger triangle?
options: 35 cm
27 cm
questions.explanation: Since both triangles contain a right angle and θ, they are similar, so sin θ = 9/15 = 0.6 in both. Then hypotenuse = 21 ÷ 0.6 = 35 cm, which also matches the scale factor 21/9 applied to 15. The answer 27 cm comes from adding the increase of 12 cm to 15 cm instead of multiplying by the scale factor, which would change the angle. Remember that similar triangles scale by multiplication, so set up equal ratios such as 9/15 = 21/h.

questions.stem: A triangle is enlarged by a scale factor of 3. What happens to the sizes of its angles?
options: Only the largest angle changes; the others stay the same
Every angle stays exactly the same size as in the original
Every angle becomes three times its original size
Every angle becomes one third of its original size
questions.explanation: An enlargement multiplies every length by the scale factor but leaves the shape unchanged, so the image is similar to the original and corresponding angles are equal. The tempting answer is that every angle becomes three times its original size, but tripling angles would distort the shape (and the angle sum of a triangle must stay 180°). The cue: scale factor acts on lengths only, never on angles.

questions.stem: In an enlargement, the scale factor is found by calculating:
options: image length − matching original length
image length × matching original length
image length ÷ matching original length
original length ÷ matching image length
questions.explanation: Scale factor k satisfies image length = k × original length, so k is the image length divided by the corresponding original length. Dividing the original by the image reverses the ratio and gives the scale factor of the enlargement that maps the image back to the original. Subtracting gives a difference in centimetres, not a ratio, so it would change if the units changed.

questions.stem: A shape is enlarged by a scale factor of 2. Compared with the original, the area of the image is:
options: 4 times the original area
2 times the original area
8 times the original area
the same as the original area
questions.explanation: Area depends on two dimensions, so if each length doubles the area is multiplied by 2 × 2 = 4. The common error is answering 2 times, applying the length scale factor directly to area. The cue: lengths scale by k, areas by k², volumes by k³.

questions.stem: A quadrilateral is enlarged using a scale factor of ½. Which statement about the image is correct?
options: It is smaller than the original and no longer similar to it
It is larger than the original because enlargements always enlarge
It has the same side lengths but half the angle sizes
It is smaller than the original but similar to it
questions.explanation: A scale factor between 0 and 1 produces a reduction, but every length is still multiplied by the same number and angles are unchanged, so the image is similar to the original. The tempting choice is that it is smaller and no longer similar, but similarity only requires equal angles and a constant ratio of corresponding sides, which is exactly what a scale factor of ½ gives. Remember that 'enlargement' is the name of the transformation, not a guarantee that the image grows.

questions.stem: When a shape is enlarged about a centre of enlargement O, which point does not move?
options: The vertex of the shape closest to O
The centre of the original shape
The midpoint of the longest side
The centre O itself
questions.explanation: Every point P maps to a point on the ray from O through P at k times the distance from O, so the only point whose distance from O is unchanged is O itself (its distance is zero). Choosing the vertex nearest O is tempting because it moves least, but unless it sits exactly on O it still moves outwards by the scale factor. The cue: the fixed point is the centre, not the closest point.

questions.stem: A pentagon with perimeter 30 cm is enlarged by a scale factor of 4. The perimeter of the image is:
options: 480 cm
7.5 cm
120 cm
34 cm
questions.explanation: Perimeter is a sum of lengths, and every length is multiplied by the scale factor, so the perimeter is also multiplied by 4: 30 × 4 = 120 cm. The answer 480 cm comes from using 4² = 16, which is the area factor, not the length factor. Perimeter scales like a length; only area needs the squared factor.

questions.stem: A rectangle measuring 4 cm by 6 cm is enlarged by a scale factor of 2.5. The dimensions of the image are:
options: 10 cm by 6 cm
1.6 cm by 2.4 cm
10 cm by 15 cm
6.5 cm by 8.5 cm
questions.explanation: Both dimensions are multiplied by the same scale factor: 4 × 2.5 = 10 and 6 × 2.5 = 15. Choosing 10 cm by 6 cm applies the factor to one side only, which would change the shape's proportions and destroy similarity. In an enlargement every length, in every direction, is multiplied by the same number.

questions.stem: Triangle ABC has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. Its image under an enlargement has sides 15 cm, 20 cm and 25 cm. The scale factor is:
questions.explanation: Divide any image length by its matching original length: 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5, and 20 ÷ 8 and 25 ÷ 10 give the same value, confirming the shapes are similar. The answer 9 comes from subtracting 6 from 15, treating the change as additive instead of multiplicative. Check your factor on all three pairs of sides — a genuine enlargement gives the same ratio every time.

questions.stem: A shape with area 12 cm² is enlarged by a scale factor of 3. The area of the image is:
options: 108 cm²
36 cm²
324 cm²
15 cm²
questions.explanation: Area is multiplied by the square of the scale factor, so 12 × 3² = 12 × 9 = 108 cm². The answer 36 cm² comes from multiplying the area by 3 instead of by 9, which is the most common slip. Ask yourself how many dimensions the measurement involves: two dimensions means squaring the factor.

questions.stem: Two similar shapes have areas of 2 cm² and 50 cm². What is the scale factor of the enlargement from the smaller to the larger?
questions.explanation: The area ratio is 50 ÷ 2 = 25, and since area scales by k², the length scale factor is √25 = 5. Answering 25 stops at the area ratio and forgets to take the square root. The cue: to go from an area ratio back to a length ratio, take the square root.

questions.stem: In dynamic geometry software a shape is enlarged about centre O with scale factor 1.5. A vertex P of the original sits 4 cm from O. How far from O is its image P'?
options: 5.5 cm
2.7 cm
4 cm
6 cm
questions.explanation: Under an enlargement, the distance of every image point from the centre is the scale factor times the original distance: 4 × 1.5 = 6 cm, with P' on the ray OP. The answer 5.5 cm comes from adding 1.5 cm rather than multiplying by 1.5. Scale factors always multiply distances from the centre.

questions.stem: Which statement is always true?
options: Any two rhombuses are similar to each other
Any two isosceles triangles are similar to each other
Any two squares are similar to each other
Any two rectangles are similar to each other
questions.explanation: All squares have four 90° angles and four equal sides, so any square can be mapped onto any other by an enlargement — the ratio of corresponding sides is the same in every direction. Rectangles are the tempting choice, but a 1 cm by 2 cm rectangle and a 1 cm by 5 cm rectangle have different side ratios, so they are not similar. Similarity needs equal angles and a single constant ratio for all corresponding sides.

questions.stem: A cube of side 2 cm is enlarged by a scale factor of 3. Compared with the original, the volume of the image is:
options: 27 times as large
3 times as large
9 times as large
6 times as large
questions.explanation: Volume involves three dimensions, so it is multiplied by the cube of the scale factor: 3³ = 27 (the volume goes from 8 cm³ to 216 cm³). Answering 9 times uses the squared factor, which applies to surface area, not volume. Match the power to the number of dimensions: 1 for length, 2 for area, 3 for volume.

questions.stem: A shape is enlarged about a centre O using a scale factor of −2. Which description of the image is correct?
options: It is twice as large and lies on the opposite side of O, rotated 180°
It is twice as large and lies on the same side of O as the original
It is half as large and lies on the opposite side of O
It is twice as large and is a mirror reflection in a line through O
questions.explanation: A negative scale factor sends each point to the opposite side of the centre along the same line, at 2 times the distance, which is the same as an enlargement by 2 combined with a 180° rotation about O. Saying it is a mirror reflection is tempting because the image looks flipped, but a reflection reverses orientation, whereas a 180° rotation preserves it. The size comes from the magnitude of the factor and the side comes from its sign.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the sine ratio of an acute angle θ is defined as:
options: the length of the side opposite θ divided by the hypotenuse
the length of the side adjacent to θ divided by the hypotenuse
the length of the side opposite θ divided by the side adjacent to θ
the length of the hypotenuse divided by the side opposite θ
questions.explanation: Sine compares the side facing the angle with the hypotenuse: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse. The version using the adjacent side and hypotenuse is the cosine ratio, which is the most common mix-up because both use the hypotenuse. The clue is the word 'opposite' — sine always looks across the triangle at the side facing θ, while cosine looks at the side beside it.

questions.stem: For an acute angle θ in a right-angled triangle, the value of sin θ depends on:
options: the size of θ only, and not on how large the triangle is drawn
the length of the hypotenuse only, and not on the size of θ
both the size of θ and the perimeter of the particular triangle
the size of θ and the scale factor used when drawing the triangle
questions.explanation: All right-angled triangles containing the same acute angle θ are similar (equal angles), so their corresponding sides are in the same ratio and opposite ÷ hypotenuse gives one fixed number for that angle. The option mentioning the size of θ and the scale factor is tempting because larger drawings do have longer sides, but enlarging multiplies both the opposite side and the hypotenuse by the same factor, leaving the quotient unchanged. Remember: side lengths change with size, ratios do not.

questions.stem: Three right-angled triangles each have a 27° angle. In each, opposite ÷ hypotenuse gives results that are:
options: identical, because the three triangles are similar
in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3, matching the hypotenuses
steadily larger, because the opposite side gets longer
all different, since only the angles match, not the sides
questions.explanation: Each triangle has a right angle and a 27° angle, so the third angles match too and the triangles are similar; corresponding sides are therefore in a constant ratio and opposite ÷ hypotenuse is the same number every time. The answer '1 : 2 : 3, matching the hypotenuses' confuses side lengths, which really are in that ratio, with the quotient of two sides, which is not. Check whether a question asks for a length or for a ratio of two lengths.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, an acute angle θ has tan θ = 5/12. A similar right-angled triangle has its side adjacent to θ measuring 36 cm. The side opposite θ in the larger triangle is:
options: 39 cm
60 cm
15 cm
29 cm
questions.explanation: Because the triangles are similar, tan θ keeps the value 5/12, so opposite ÷ 36 = 5/12, giving opposite = 36 × 5 ÷ 12 = 15 cm. Choosing 60 cm comes from multiplying by 5 and forgetting to divide by 12, that is, treating 12 → 36 as if the scale factor were 5. The scale factor here is 36 ÷ 12 = 3, so the opposite side is 3 × 5.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has an acute angle θ with cos θ = 8/17. A similar right-angled triangle containing θ has a hypotenuse of 51 cm. The side adjacent to θ in the larger triangle is:
options: 34 cm
42 cm
24 cm
30 cm
questions.explanation: Similar triangles share the same cosine for θ, so adjacent ÷ 51 = 8/17, giving adjacent = 51 × 8 ÷ 17 = 24 cm. The value 34 cm comes from mistakenly using the difference 51 − 17 = 34 instead of the scale factor 51 ÷ 17 = 3. Enlargement is multiplicative, so always divide to find the scale factor, then multiply.

questions.stem: Triangle A is right-angled with legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Triangle B is right-angled with legs 8 cm and 10 cm. A student claims the two triangles have the same sine, cosine and tangent values. The correct response is:
options: the claim is wrong, because 6/8 does not equal 8/10, so the triangles are not similar
the claim is right, because both are right-angled and both contain a side of 8 cm
the claim is right, because both triangles have whole-number legs and a right angle
the claim is wrong, because trigonometric ratios only match when the triangles are identical
questions.explanation: Two right-angled triangles are similar only when their pairs of legs are in the same ratio; here 6/8 = 0.75 but 8/10 = 0.8, so the acute angles differ and so do the ratios. The response about sharing a side of 8 cm is tempting, but a shared side length says nothing about the angles — it is the ratio of the two legs that fixes them. Similar triangles need not be identical, only in proportion, which is why the last option is also false.

questions.stem: For any acute angle θ in a right-angled triangle, sin θ must be less than 1. The reason is:
options: θ is always less than 90°, and ratios formed from angles under 90° stay under 1
the side opposite θ is always shorter than the side adjacent to θ in such triangles
the hypotenuse is the shortest side, so dividing by it always gives a small answer
the hypotenuse is the longest side, so the opposite side divided by it is under 1
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse sits opposite the right angle and is always the longest side, so opposite ÷ hypotenuse is a smaller number divided by a larger one, giving a value below 1. The explanation based on θ being less than 90° confuses the size of the angle with the size of the ratio — the ratio is about side lengths, not degrees. Note that the opposite side is not always shorter than the adjacent side, since for θ greater than 45° it is longer, so that reasoning fails too.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has a fixed angle θ. As it is drawn larger, what happens to opposite ÷ hypotenuse?
options: It doubles each time the hypotenuse doubles, matching the scale factor
It stays exactly the same, because all such triangles are similar
It increases in proportion to the hypotenuse, as the opposite side grows
It decreases, because the hypotenuse grows faster than the opposite side
questions.explanation: All right-angled triangles containing the same acute angle θ are similar by AA, so corresponding sides are in the same proportion and the opposite-to-hypotenuse ratio is fixed for that angle. The idea that it doubles when the hypotenuse doubles is the common trap: both sides are multiplied by the scale factor, so the factor cancels in the ratio. Cue: enlargement changes lengths but never changes angles or ratios of corresponding sides.

questions.stem: Using sin 40° ≈ 0.643, a right-angled triangle with a 40° angle has a hypotenuse of 12 cm. The length of the side opposite the 40° angle is closest to:
options: 4.8 cm
7.7 cm
questions.explanation: Since opposite ÷ hypotenuse is the constant 0.643 for every right-angled triangle with a 40° angle, the opposite side is 0.643 × 12 ≈ 7.7 cm. The 18.7 cm answer comes from dividing 12 by 0.643, which treats the hypotenuse as the opposite side. Cue: the opposite side must be shorter than the hypotenuse, so multiplying by a ratio less than 1 is the correct move.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has sides 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm. A similar triangle has its shortest side 35 cm. In the larger triangle, the cosine of the angle between the longer leg and the hypotenuse is:
questions.explanation: For that angle the adjacent side is the longer leg and the hypotenuse is the longest side, so cosine is 24/25 = 0.96 in the small triangle, and similarity means the value is identical in the larger one (120/125 = 0.96). The 4.80 option comes from multiplying 0.96 by the scale factor 5, but ratios are unchanged by enlargement. The 0.28 value is 7/25, which is the sine of that angle, not the cosine.

questions.stem: Triangle 1 is right-angled with a side of 4 cm opposite angle θ and a hypotenuse of 7 cm. Triangle 2 is right-angled with a side of 10 cm opposite one of its acute angles and a hypotenuse of 17.5 cm. What can be concluded?
options: That acute angle in Triangle 2 equals θ, since 10/17.5 = 4/7
The angles must differ, since the side lengths are not equal
No conclusion is possible, because the scale factor 2.5 is not a whole number
No conclusion is possible until both angles are measured with a protractor
questions.explanation: Because opposite ÷ hypotenuse is 4/7 ≈ 0.571 in both triangles, the triangles are similar (the third sides are in the same ratio too), so the angles correspond and are equal. Saying the angles must differ because the sides differ confuses size with shape: enlargement changes lengths while keeping every angle the same. Equal ratios of corresponding sides is exactly the evidence needed — no measuring is required.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has an acute angle θ with the opposite side 15 cm, the adjacent side 8 cm and the hypotenuse 17 cm. A second, similar right-angled triangle has a perimeter three times as large. What is the value of tan θ in the larger triangle?
options: 1.875, since tan θ is unchanged by the enlargement
5.625, since every length is tripled by the enlargement
0.533, since the larger triangle reverses the two legs
0.882, since the hypotenuse grows with the opposite side
questions.explanation: Similar triangles have all corresponding sides in the same ratio, so tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent = 15/8 = 1.875 in both triangles; the common factor of 3 cancels (45/24 = 1.875). The answer 5.625 is the tempting trap: it multiplies the ratio by the scale factor, but tripling both numerator and denominator leaves the quotient unchanged. The value 0.533 comes from writing adjacent ÷ opposite, and 0.882 uses 15/17, which is sin θ. Cue: a trigonometric ratio depends only on the size of the angle, never on how big the triangle is drawn.

questions.stem: What is a transversal?
options: A line of symmetry through a shape
A line joining two opposite corners
A line touching a circle at one point
A line crossing two or more other lines
questions.explanation: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, the angle pairs it creates — corresponding, alternate and co-interior — are what most geometric reasoning questions are built on.
questions.teaching:
Angle reasoning around parallel lines depends on one line cutting across the others, and that line has its own name.

Where it crosses parallel lines it creates eight angles in two matching groups of four, and the relationships between them are what geometry proofs are built on. Corresponding angles sit in matching positions and are equal. Alternate angles sit on opposite sides between the parallels and are equal. Co-interior angles sit on the same side between them and add to a straight line. Identifying the crossing line first is what makes those patterns visible.

questions.stem: What do co-interior angles on parallel lines add to?
options: 360 degrees
They are equal
180 degrees
90 degrees
questions.explanation: Co-interior angles sit on the same side of the transversal, between the parallel lines, and they are supplementary. Alternate and corresponding angles are equal instead, which is the pair usually confused with this one.
questions.teaching:
Three angle relationships appear whenever a line crosses parallel lines, and two of them behave one way while the third behaves differently.

Corresponding angles — in matching positions at each intersection — are equal. Alternate angles — on opposite sides of the crossing line, between the parallels — are also equal. The third pair sits on the *same* side of the crossing line, between the parallels, and these do not match: together they complete a straight line. Remembering that two of the three are equal and one is supplementary is the fastest way to keep them apart.

questions.stem: What is a diagonal of a polygon?
options: A line joining two neighbouring corners
A line from a corner to the midpoint of a side
A line parallel to one of the sides
A line joining two non-adjacent corners
questions.explanation: Joining neighbouring corners just traces a side, so a diagonal has to skip at least one vertex. Counting them is a standard way into reasoning about how many triangles a polygon divides into.
questions.teaching:
Polygons are described using vertices and sides, and there is a specific term for a line drawn inside one.

Joining two vertices that are next to each other simply retraces a side, so it does not count. The lines that do count skip at least one vertex, cutting across the interior. They matter because they divide a polygon into triangles, and since every triangle's angles total 180 degrees, counting those triangles gives you the angle sum of any polygon. A quadrilateral splits into two, a pentagon into three, and so on.

questions.stem: What does a scale factor of 2 do to a shape?
options: Doubles every length
Doubles the area
Doubles the number of sides
Halves every length
questions.explanation: The scale factor applies to lengths directly. Area is multiplied by the factor squared and volume by the factor cubed, so doubling lengths quadruples area — which is the step most often missed.
questions.teaching:
Enlargement multiplies lengths by a factor, and the crucial point is that area and volume do not follow the same multiplier.

Every length in the shape — sides, heights, diagonals, radii — is multiplied by the factor directly. Area, being two dimensions, is multiplied by the factor squared. Volume, being three, is multiplied by the factor cubed. So doubling the lengths of a shape quadruples the area it covers and gives eight times the volume. Missing that step is the single most common error in scaling questions, and it is worth checking which quantity is being asked for.

questions.stem: What is the exterior angle of a triangle equal to?
options: The two opposite interior angles added
The nearest interior angle
Ninety degrees always
The largest interior angle
questions.explanation: Because interior angles total 180 and the exterior angle completes a straight line with its neighbour, what is left is exactly the other two interior angles combined.
questions.teaching:
Extending one side of a triangle creates an angle outside it, and there is a neat relationship worth knowing.

Two facts combine to produce it. The three interior angles total 180 degrees, and the exterior angle sits on a straight line with its adjacent interior angle, so those two also total 180. Set those equal and the adjacent interior angle cancels, leaving the exterior angle equal to the sum of the two it is not touching. That saves a step compared with working out the interior angle first, and it appears constantly in geometric proofs.

questions.stem: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
questions.explanation: Two run through the midpoints of opposite sides and two along the diagonals. A rectangle that is not square has only the first two, which is where the answer 2 comes from.
questions.teaching:
A line of symmetry is a fold line: reflect the shape across it and the two halves match exactly.

Finding all of them for a shape means testing every possible fold. For a rectangle, folding through the midpoints of opposite sides works both ways, but folding along a diagonal does not — the corners miss. A square is a rectangle where the sides are equal, and that extra equality makes the diagonal folds work as well. So a square has everything a rectangle has, plus more, which is exactly where the difference between the two answers comes from.
